title: The King on a Donkey
sum: The second half of the book opens with an oracle that sweeps down from northern Syria through Damascus, Tyre and Sidon to the four Philistine cities, as if a conqueror were marching south. The LORD humbles the proud trading power of Tyre, strikes the Philistine cities, and takes the survivors in as a remnant that joins Judah (9:1-8). Then the tone turns: Daughter Zion is told to shout, because her king is coming, righteous and rescued, poor and riding a donkey. He will take away chariots, horses and war bows, speak peace to the nations, and rule from sea to sea (9:9-10).

The rest of the chapter is the LORD at war for his people. He frees the prisoners of hope by the blood of the covenant, bends Judah like a bow against Greece, appears over his people like lightning and sounds the ram's horn, and shields them. At the end they are jewels in a crown, and grain and new wine make the young bloom (9:11-17). Matthew 21 and John 12 both quote 9:9 at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.
readings: Read as the LORD's own campaign

The chapter is a single march of the LORD the divine warrior from the north to the south of the land (9:1-8), with the king as his agent of peace (9:9-10) and the LORD himself at the head of the battle (9:13-15). The poor king and the war are two faces of the same rule.
Read as a prophecy of the coming king

Jewish and Christian readers have both taken 9:9-10 as a promise of the Messiah, humble and yet ruling to the ends of the earth. The Gospels apply 9:9 to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, and the Talmud has the Messiah come as a poor man on a donkey if Israel is not worthy (Sanhedrin 98a).
Read as the hope of its own time

Critical readers see a poem of the Persian or Greek period that promised a lasting king after the failure of Zerubbabel's line, and a victory over Greek or Phoenician power. The poem does not name the king, and its 'I will cut off' (9:10) is the LORD's own act.

views.H: Three settings are argued. (1) Alexander the Great's march in 333-332 BC, which seized the treasure at Damascus, accepted Sidon's surrender, took Tyre after a siege and took Gaza after another. (2) The Assyrian campaigns of the 8th century BC, which took the same lands. (3) The Persian period, when the coastal cities were Persian subjects. 'Greece' in 9:13 suits a Greek date best, but Greeks were known in Judah's world long before Alexander. Nothing in the chapter is dated.
views.C: Most critical scholars think chapters 9-14 are separate from 1-8, with no dates, no Zerubbabel or Joshua, and a different style. Stade (1881-82) dated chapters 9-14 to the Greek period, and Hanson put the roots of apocalyptic here. Meyers and Meyers read the chapters against the background of the Greco-Persian wars. Some conservative scholars keep Zechariah as author and read Greece as the western rival of Persia. The Hebrew of 9:5-8 and 9:15-16 is hard.
views.J: The rabbis took 9:9 of the Messiah. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) sets the two pictures of Daniel 7:13 (the Messiah coming with the clouds of heaven) and Zechariah 9:9 (the poor man on a donkey) side by side, and says it depends on whether Israel is worthy. The Hadrach wordplay of R. Judah, 'harsh to the nations, tender to Israel' (9:1; Sifre Deuteronomy, Pisqa 1), is a rabbinic reading of the first verse.
views.X: The Gospels quote 9:9 at Jesus' entry (Matthew 21:1-9; John 12:12-16). Cyril of Alexandria comments on the chapter in his commentary on the Twelve and applies the king of 9:9 to Christ. Palm Sunday keeps the entry in the liturgy of the Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches.
views.F: Many Christian readers divide the chapter: the entry fulfilled 9:9, and 9:10 (the end of war, rule from sea to sea) waits for the second coming. Others read both verses as fulfilled in Christ's present reign. Jewish messianic hope expects the whole chapter.

deep.b: The verses move without a break from description ('your king is coming') to the LORD's own voice ('I will cut off the chariot') and back to the king ('he will speak peace'). The LORD removes the weapons and the king speaks peace; the two acts belong together, and the king's rule 'from sea to sea' is the royal psalm's language (Psalm 72:8). The king himself brings no army and no horse, which is a pointed contrast to the kings who trusted them (Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1). That is why the Gospel writers could find his mark in a man on a young donkey.
deep.refs: Psalm 72:8; Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1; Hosea 1:7; Matthew 21:1-9; John 12:12-16

echoes: Matthew 21:1-9; John 12:12-16; Mark 11:1-10; Luke 19:28-40; Zephaniah 3:14-17; Isaiah 62:11; Genesis 49:10-11; Psalm 72:8; Exodus 24:8; Micah 5:4, 10; Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:6-10; Ezekiel 26-28; Zechariah 10:6; 14:3

settings.what: The oracle against Hadrach, Damascus, Tyre and Philistia
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah (the small Persian province of Yehud), gathered around the rebuilt Temple, and the scattered Judeans and northerners abroad
settings.when: Not dated. Alexander's campaign of 333-332 BC, an Assyrian setting in the 8th century BC, and a Persian setting are all argued.
settings.why: To tell a small, weak community that the great trading and military powers on its borders will fall, that the LORD himself will camp at his house as guard, and that even the old enemy Philistia will have a remnant among his people. Reading it as spoken to the people of Yehud, the oracle is not a call to arms but an assurance. The nations are spoken about, not to.
views: Alexander's march, 332 BC
The order of cities matches the campaign, Damascus and Sidon, Tyre, then Gaza. Those who hold it often date the whole of chapters 9-14 to the Greek period.
An earlier, Assyrian setting
The cities and kings (Hadrach, Hamath, Gaza's king) fit the campaigns of Tiglath-pileser III and his successors in the 8th century BC.
A Persian-period oracle
A prophet of Zechariah's own time could use the old list as a pattern of judgment on the neighbors, as Amos 1-2 did, without naming a particular conquest.

settings.what: The coming king: poor, on a donkey, bringing peace
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: Daughter Zion and Daughter Jerusalem, the city and its people, addressed as a woman told to shout for joy
settings.when: Not dated; the verses speak of a future day ('look, your king is coming').
settings.why: To turn a people used to trusting horses, chariots and bows to a king who brings none of them. The king is not named, and a poor king on a donkey is the opposite of a conqueror. The promise of peace to the nations and of a rule to the ends of the earth also gives the small province a hope beyond its own borders. For the first hearers, the words held out a king after the failure of the royal line to return (compare Haggai 2:23); for later readers, a figure to look for.
views: A Davidic king still to come (Jewish and Christian messianic readings)
The Talmud, the Gospels and the fathers all take the king as the Messiah, differing on who he is.
An ideal ruler of the prophet's own time
Some critical readers think the poem pictures a hoped-for king of the Persian or Greek period and does not name him.
The LORD himself as the king
The shift between 'I' and 'he' (9:10) leads some to hear the king as the LORD's own presence, the 'king' of 14:9.

settings.what: The prisoners of hope and the LORD's war
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: Zion and the scattered people, the 'prisoners' held in exile or in the pit
settings.when: Not dated; the 'sons of Greece' (9:13) suggest, to many, a Greek-period setting.
settings.why: To promise release for the scattered, a double portion for those who waited, and victory over a stronger power. It tells the community that its smallness is not the end: the LORD will use Judah and Ephraim as bow and arrow, and then settle them in plenty. Hearers who lived under foreign power would hear both a war promise and a harvest promise.
views: The Maccabean wars
Some read 9:13-15 as a reflection of the wars against the Seleucid Greeks in the 160s BC, which would date the passage late.
An earlier war poem
Others read it as an older war poem of the LORD with Greece as a distant, far-western people.
A hope not tied to one event
The imagery is the traditional picture of the divine warrior (Habakkuk 3; Psalm 18) and need not describe a particular war.

traditions.q: Is the king on a donkey (9:9) fulfilled at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, and what of the rest of 9:10?
views: Catholic

Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey manifests the coming of the kingdom, won not by violence but by the humility that bears witness to the truth; the Church opens Holy Week with Palm Sunday (Catechism 559-560).
catechism-catholic
Orthodox

The Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem is one of the Twelve Great Feasts, kept on the Sunday before Pascha with palms or willow branches blessed, and the Church sees in it Christ the King coming to his Passion and the sign of the victory over death shown at the raising of Lazarus the day before. Cyril of Alexandria, whose commentary on the Twelve Prophets is read in the Greek church, takes the king of 9:9 to be Christ and sees in the call to rejoice the end of the sadness that sin and death had brought.
cyril-twelve
Reformed

Calvin reads 9:9-10 of Christ and says there would be no horses, chariots or bows in his kingdom, since God himself restrains the rage of its enemies and gives peace, so that the Messiah's safety does not rest on human defenses.
calvin-twelve
Dispensationalist

The entry is the king's presentation of himself to Israel, the end of the sixty-nine weeks of Daniel 9:25, which Harold Hoehner dates to the triumphal entry, and the second half of the prophecy, the rule from sea to sea and the end of war, waits for the second coming and the millennial kingdom.
hoehner-chronological

title: Sheep Without a Shepherd
sum: The second chapter of the first oracle begins with a call to pray for rain. The LORD sends rain in its season, and the teraphim and diviners of the people give only empty answers, so that the people wander like sheep with no shepherd (10:1-2). The LORD's anger burns against the shepherds, the rulers, and he will take care of his flock, making Judah like a war horse (10:3-5).

The second half promises that the LORD will strengthen Judah and Joseph, bring them home because he has compassion on them, whistle them in from Egypt and Assyria, and sow them among the peoples so that they will remember him. The sea is struck, the Nile's depths dry up, and the pride of Assyria falls (10:6-12). The chapter ends in the same strength that begins it, in the name of the LORD.
readings: Read as a promise of return

The chapter pictures the scattered northerners and southerners coming home together and being so many that there is no room for them. It is the Exodus again, with Assyria and Egypt as the old powers that must give them up.
Read as a charge against leaders
The first half and the last of 10:2-3 aim at shepherds and goats, the rulers, who led the people to teraphim and false dreams. The LORD will deal with them in person.
Read as a prophecy of the church
Christian writers have heard in 'I will whistle to them and gather them in' (10:8) the call of the gospel to the nations, and in the cornerstone of 10:4 Christ.

views.H: Ephraim (the north) went into exile in 722 BC and Judah in 586 BC. In the Persian period most northerners and many southerners were still scattered in Egypt, Assyria's old lands and Babylon. The chapter speaks to a community that knew itself as a fragment. The drought and failed rains of 10:1 are the same kind of lack that Haggai 1:10-11 describes.
views.C: Many critical scholars see 10:3b-12 as a unit about the return of Ephraim and treat 10:1-3a as a separate piece on shepherds, that was joined to chapter 11. The list in 10:10-11 (Egypt, Assyria) may be traditional, or, as some critical commentators think, may stand for Ptolemaic Egypt and Seleucid Syria. 'The sea of trouble' (10:11) is textually uncertain.
views.J: Jewish readers have taken the return of Ephraim and Judah together as the end-time ingathering of the exiles, the 'ten tribes' included. The call to pray for rain in the season is picked up by the prayer for rain on Shemini Atzeret (Mishnah Taanit 1:1 on when rain is first mentioned).
views.X: The church fathers read the shepherds as the leaders who failed Israel and the new flock as the church of Jews and Gentiles. Jesus saw the crowds as sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36), and John 10 sets the good shepherd against hired men.
views.F: Dispensationalist and other premillennial readers take 10:6-12 as the regathering of all Israel before or at the second coming. Others read it as fulfilled in the spread of the gospel. Jewish messianic hope looks for the return of the northern tribes.

echoes: Matthew 9:36; Mark 6:34; John 10:11-16; Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Jeremiah 23:1-4; Ezekiel 34:1-31; Hosea 2:23; Hosea 11:10-11; Isaiah 11:11-16; Exodus 14-15; Jeremiah 31:1-9

settings.what: Ask for rain: the false guides and the shepherds
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah (the small Persian province of Yehud), gathered around the rebuilt Temple, and the scattered Judeans and northerners abroad (the leaders, the 'shepherds' and 'lead goats,' are spoken of in the third person)
settings.when: Not dated; the rain of the 'spring' season is the setting.
settings.why: To say that rain and harvest come from the LORD, not from teraphim, diviners or dreamers, who have left the people to wander like sheep. The command to the people is simply 'Ask,' and the warning is at the shepherds. Knowing the hearers were a farming community that had suffered poor harvests (Haggai 1:10-11) makes the call about rain a call to trust.
views: Baal as rain-giver
The call may be aimed at Canaanite rain religion; the LORD, not Baal, makes the storm clouds.
The shepherds as foreign rulers
Some read the 'shepherds' as Persian or Greek officials; the Hebrew word covers any ruler.

settings.what: The LORD brings Judah and Joseph home
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: The scattered people of both halves of Israel: 'the house of Judah' and 'the house of Joseph,' with Ephraim
settings.when: Not dated; the return from Egypt and Assyria is the picture.
settings.why: To promise that the split of 1 Kings 12 and the scattering of 722 and 586 BC will be undone: the LORD made them strong, saves, brings them back and gathers them 'because I have compassion on them.' For a community that was only Judah, it held out a hope for a reunited people. The old exodus images (the sea struck, the river dried) show what kind of act it will be.
views: A return from the Persian and Egyptian diasporas
The hope speaks of the Jews scattered in Egypt and the East after the exile.
The lost ten tribes
Later readers took 'Joseph' as the northern tribes lost in Assyria and expected their return (see the topic).

title: Two Staffs and Thirty Shekels
sum: The chapter opens with a funeral song: fire in the cedars of Lebanon, wailing in the oaks of Bashan, and the shepherds wailing because their glory is ruined (11:1-3). Then the LORD tells the prophet to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter, whose buyers kill them unpunished and whose own shepherds have no pity (11:4-6). The prophet takes two staffs, Favor and Union, gets rid of three shepherds in a month, loses patience with the flock and is hated by them, and breaks Favor, which cancels the covenant with the peoples (11:7-11).

Asked for his wages, he is given thirty shekels of silver. The LORD says, 'Throw it to the potter,' and he throws it into the house of the LORD. Then he breaks Union, the brotherhood between Judah and Israel (11:12-14). Finally he is told to take the tools of a foolish shepherd, for the LORD will raise up a shepherd who leaves the flock, and a sword will strike his arm and eye (11:15-17). Matthew 27:3-10 quotes 11:12-13 at Judas's payment.
readings: Read as the story of the LORD's rejected shepherding

The prophet plays the part of the LORD, the true shepherd of Israel (Ezekiel 34), whom the flock and its leaders reject. His wage is an insult, the breaking of the two staffs is the end of the covenant of favor and of the unity of the people, and the foolish shepherd is the ruler God allows in his place.
Read as history of the prophet's own time

Critical readers take the passage as a coded history of leadership in Judah in the Persian or Greek period: three rulers removed in a short time, a flock sold by its owners, a division between Judah and the north or the Samaritans. We cannot now name the people, but the first readers could.
Read as a picture of the rejected Christ

Christian readers have read the shepherd as Christ rejected and sold for thirty shekels (Matthew 26:15; 27:9-10), the breaking of Favor as the end of the old covenant, and the foolish shepherd as the false leaders or Antichrist. Matthew's own use is narrower: he quotes the payment and the potter.

views.H: There is no agreed historical referent. Proposals include the last kings of Judah (Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin), Persian governors and high priests, the Seleucid-era High Priests, and Ptolemaic rulers, all with 'three shepherds' in a month. The story of a purchased field in Jeremiah 32 and a potter's house in Jeremiah 18 are the background to Matthew's use.
views.C: This is the most disputed chapter of the book. The Hebrew is rough in 11:4-14, a sign act is told in the first person, and the three shepherds, the traders (11:5) and the potter are not explained. Hanson reads chapters 9-14 as the work of visionaries, a group out of power in the postexilic community, and some scholars read the shepherd passages as a critique of the community's leaders. The Septuagint has 'the Canaanite land' (11:7) and 'the Canaanites' (11:11) where the Hebrew has 'the poor of the flock' and 'furnace' for 'potter' (11:13); see the variants.
views.J: The Talmud reads the three shepherds as Moses, Aaron and Miriam (Taanit 9a), and tells the story of the Temple doors that opened by themselves in the last forty years before the destruction with the verse 'Open your doors, Lebanon' (11:1; Yoma 39b). The Talmud lists Jeremiah first among the Latter Prophets (Bava Batra 14b).
views.X: The fathers read 11:12-13 of the sale of Jesus and the potter's field (Matthew 27:3-10), and 11:15-17 of Antichrist or the false shepherds (John 10:12-13). Jerome reports a Jeremiah apocryphon among the Nazarenes with the Matthew quotation in it, but thinks the testimony more likely taken from Zechariah; Augustine and Calvin differ on how to explain the name. See the card.
views.F: Some premillennial readers take the foolish shepherd of 11:15-17 as the Antichrist of the last days, and the three shepherds as three rulers removed before the end. Others see only the passage's use in Matthew.

deep.h: Thirty shekels, a potter and a field
deep.b: Three Old Testament places meet in Matthew's single quotation. In Exodus 21:32 thirty shekels is the compensation for a slave killed by an ox. In Zechariah 11:12-13 the same sum is the wage of the shepherd, thrown to the potter in the house of the LORD. In Jeremiah 18-19 the prophet visits the potter's house and breaks a potter's jar in the valley where the innocent were killed (Jeremiah 19:4, 10), and in Jeremiah 32 he buys a field with silver weighed on a scale. Matthew's story has Judas throw the silver into the sanctuary, the priests refuse it as blood money and buy the Potter's Field for strangers' graves. Acts 1:18-19 tells a different story about the same field. Each of these places is part of what the single quotation 'Jeremiah' covers.
deep.refs: Exodus 21:32; Zechariah 11:12-13; Jeremiah 18:1-6; Jeremiah 19:1-13; Jeremiah 32:6-15; Matthew 27:3-10; Acts 1:18-19

deep.title: The poor king and the poor flock (Claude's theory)
deep.b: The Hebrew word 'ani, 'poor,' appears in three places in this part of the book: the king of 9:9 is poor, and the flock he shepherds in 11:7 and 11:11 are 'the poor of the flock.' It does not appear in chapters 12-14. A possible reading: the poor king of 9:9 is the shepherd of the poor flock in chapter 11, and the flock recognizes 'the word of the LORD' only when his staff is broken (11:11). The shepherd who is paid thirty shekels (11:12), the pierced one (12:10) and the struck shepherd (13:7) would then be one figure seen in three scenes. The text does not say so, and many commentators keep the figures separate. I offer it as a link made by one Hebrew word, not as a settled result.

echoes: Matthew 27:3-10; Matthew 26:15; Acts 1:18-19; Exodus 21:32; Jeremiah 18-19; Jeremiah 32:6-15; Ezekiel 34; Ezekiel 37:15-22; John 10:1-18; Jeremiah 23:1-4; Hosea 2:18; 1 Kings 22:17; Zechariah 9:9; Zechariah 13:7

settings.what: A funeral song for the forests and the shepherds
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah (the small Persian province of Yehud), gathered around the rebuilt Temple, and the scattered Judeans and northerners abroad
settings.why: To announce, in the form of a funeral cry, that the mighty trees and the shepherds who lorded it over the land are ruined. The call to 'open your doors' is not to the people but to Lebanon, whose cedar built the Temple and the palace. The poem sets the ruin of the proud before the story of the shepherd, so the hearer already knows where it ends.
views: The proud rulers
Cedars and oaks are the mighty, and the shepherds are rulers who wail because their glory is gone.
The Temple
Lebanon's wood built the Temple; the Talmud takes the opening of its doors to the fire as a sign of the destruction (Yoma 39b).

settings.what: The prophet as shepherd: two staffs, three shepherds and thirty shekels
settings.by: The LORD, giving the prophet his part, and the prophet, acting and telling it in the first person
settings.to: In the story, the poor of the flock and the three shepherds, the buyers and sellers; for the first hearers, the community of Yehud, who would see the prophet play the part
settings.when: Not dated; the story is told as a sign act that the prophet carried out over some time ('in a single month').
settings.why: To show, by acting it out, that the flock the LORD has given up to slaughter has refused its good shepherd, and that the cost is the breaking of the covenant of favor and of the unity of Judah and Israel. The insult of thirty shekels tells the hearers how their leaders price the one who cared for them. It is the story of how God's care was priced, told before the cost is paid.
views: The LORD as shepherd
The prophet acts God's own part, and the wage is God's.
A good leader of the prophet's time
A ruler or a prophet, whom we cannot name, was dismissed by the people with an insult.
Christ, the rejected shepherd
The Gospel of Matthew finds in the thirty silver coins and the potter the pattern of Jesus' betrayal.

settings.to: The prophet, who must act the part; the hearers are the community, which will have the shepherd the LORD raises
settings.when: Not dated; it follows the story of the good shepherd.
settings.why: To say that if the people refuse the good shepherd they will have the bad one, a ruler who feeds on the flock and leaves the weak. The list of what he does not do turns Ezekiel 34:4 into a charge. The woe on the worthless shepherd then promises that he will not escape.
views: A ruler of the prophet's time
A named or unnamed Persian or Greek-period ruler.
Antichrist
Early Christian writers, and later Protestants and Catholics, took the foolish shepherd as the final false ruler.

traditions.q: Why does Matthew name Jeremiah for a quotation that comes from Zechariah (Matthew 27:9-10; Zechariah 11:12-13)?
views: Catholic

Jerome says that a Nazarene Christian gave him a Hebrew book, an apocryphon of Jeremiah, with the words of Matthew in it, but he judges that the testimony was more likely taken from Zechariah, since the evangelists and apostles gave the sense and not the exact words. Augustine thinks the name Jeremiah came into Matthew's mind in place of Zechariah, and that God allowed it so that the prophets would be seen to speak with one spirit; he prefers to keep the name because most manuscripts have it.
jerome-matthew-27
augustine-harmony
Reformed

Calvin says he does not know how the name of Jeremiah came into the text and that it was put down by mistake, since the words are plainly from Zechariah; he adds that if we keep to the rule the apostles followed in quoting Scripture, the passage is highly applicable to Christ.
calvin-evangelists
Evangelical

Many evangelical commentators read it as a blended quotation: the words are Zechariah 11:12-13, joined with Jeremiah's potter and field (Jeremiah 19 and 32), and Matthew names the better-known prophet. Beale and Carson note that rabbis often named only one source for a combined quotation, and F. F. Bruce is listed with this view. Others take "Jeremiah" to stand for the whole section of the prophets, since the Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) lists him first; Barbieri, in the Bible Knowledge Commentary, is reported to say this.
christian-thinktank-matt-27-9
freebiblecommentary-matt-27-9
bavli-bava-batra

title: The One They Pierced
sum: The second oracle begins with the LORD as creator, who stretched out the heavens and formed the human spirit (12:1). He will make Jerusalem a bowl that makes the nations around her stagger and a stone too heavy to lift. All the nations gather against her, but their horses are struck with terror and blindness, Judah's clan leaders become fire in the grain, and the LORD saves the tents of Judah first so that David's house will not boast (12:2-9). The weakest among them will be like David, and David's house like the angel of the LORD.

Then the LORD pours out on David's house and Jerusalem a spirit of favor and pleading. They look to him, the one they pierced, and mourn as for an only son or a firstborn (12:10). The mourning will be as great as at Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo, and each clan mourns apart: David's house, Nathan's, Levi's, the Shimeites' and all the rest (12:11-14). John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 quote 12:10.
readings: Read as the last siege of Jerusalem

The first part is a picture of the last war: the nations come, Jerusalem is a stone that breaks them, and the LORD defends the city and its people, beginning with the countryside. It joins Ezekiel 38-39 and Joel 3.
Read as a mourning for a pierced leader

The second part turns to repentance and grief for a person who was pierced. Critical readers think of a murdered priest or prophet, the king Josiah, or an unnamed martyr. The text only says that 'they pierced' someone and that the LORD speaks of him as 'me.'
Read as a prophecy of the cross

The New Testament quotes the verse for Jesus' death and for his return. The Hebrew reading 'to me' lets Christian readers hear God himself pierced in the person of Jesus; Jewish readers hear a figure of speech or a different person.

views.H: No siege like this took place in the Persian or Greek period. Jerusalem was repeatedly attacked: by Babylon in 586, by Ptolemy I (who took it by trickery, according to Josephus, Antiquities 12.1), by Antiochus IV in 168 BC. The mourning for Josiah, killed at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:22-25), was a real national grief, and Jeremiah wrote a lament for him. A pierced figure in the poet's time is unknown.
views.C: Critical commentators divide the chapter at 12:9 or 12:10. The 'pierced one' is the main puzzle: Onias III, the high priest murdered at Daphne (2 Maccabees 4:33-34), is a candidate for those who favor a Greek date; others propose a prophet, the shepherd of 11:4-14 or 13:7, Zerubbabel, or a figure of Israel's wounded history. The Greek 'because they danced in scorn' (see the variant) shows the verb was already unclear.
views.J: The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) asks why the mourning of 12:12 is so great, and gives two answers: for the Messiah son of Joseph, who is killed, or for the evil impulse, which is slain in the days to come. Targum Jonathan has the people pray 'because they were exiled' and so does not translate 'pierced,' and Rashi reads the line as complaint to God about the Israelites whom the nations thrust through in exile, and adds the Messiah son of Joseph reading from Sukkah. Christian readers answer that the Hebrew 'to me, the one they pierced' makes the LORD the pierced one. See the note on 12:10.
views.X: John 19:37 sees the verse fulfilled when the soldier's spear pierces Jesus; Revelation 1:7 and Matthew 24:30 place the mourning at his coming. Justin Martyr used 12:10-12 to say the Jewish tribes would mourn when they saw Christ (First Apology 52). The Hebrew 'to me' has led Christians to see God himself as the pierced one in Christ.
views.F: Dispensationalist and many other premillennial readers hold that 12:10-14 describes the future national repentance of Israel at the second coming (with Romans 11:26). Others take the mourning as already happening in the conversion of Jews and Gentiles through the gospel. Jewish messianic hope expects a great mourning on the day of the Messiah.

deep.b: The Hebrew goes in one sentence from 'they will look to me' to 'they will mourn over him.' Readings: (1) One person, two ways of saying it. The LORD says 'me' and the poet then speaks of the pierced one as 'him,' as Hebrew prophecy sometimes shifts person; the LORD is wounded in his people (the commonest Christian reading, with John 19:37). (2) Two persons. The mourners look to God (me) over the matter of one they killed (him); this is the sense of Rashi, who takes it as 'about those whom the nations pierced,' and some translate 'they will look to me concerning the one they pierced.' (3) The speaker is the prophet, not the LORD. (4) 'Him' is the right reading (see the variant), which makes it simple. The verb 'pierced' does not necessarily mean death, only a violent wound, and 13:3 uses it of parents stabbing a false prophet.

echoes: John 19:37; John 19:34; Revelation 1:7; Matthew 24:30; Acts 2:17; Joel 2:28; Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 39:29; Amos 8:10; Jeremiah 6:26; Genesis 22:2; 2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:22-25; Deuteronomy 28:28; Isaiah 51:17; Obadiah 18; Luke 3:31; Numbers 3:21

settings.what: Jerusalem as a bowl and a heavy stone
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page), speaking as the creator of heaven, earth and the human spirit
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah (the small Persian province of Yehud), gathered around the rebuilt Temple, and the scattered Judeans and northerners abroad, and especially 'the clan leaders of Judah' and 'David's house' and 'the people living in Jerusalem'
settings.when: Not dated; 'on that day,' a future day of siege.
settings.why: To assure a small city and province that a siege by 'all the nations' will end in their favor, and to level the pride of the capital and the Davidic house by saving the tents of Judah first. The oracle opens with the LORD as maker so that the hearers will know who is promising. It turns the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 against their enemies.
views: A future last battle
A war of the nations against Jerusalem at the end of the age (with Ezekiel 38-39).
A traditional pattern
A type of the many sieges of Jerusalem (Isaiah 29, 36-37; Joel 3), told in the language of the divine warrior, without a particular date.

settings.what: The pouring out of the spirit and the great mourning
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page), with the LORD speaking in the first person ('they will look to me')
settings.to: David's house and the people living in Jerusalem, who are named as the mourners; the clans of David, Nathan, Levi and the Shimeites
settings.why: To say that the LORD's rescue is not the end: he will give the people a new spirit that lets them see what they have done (the 'piercing') and grieve for it, in a great family-by-family mourning. It points back to a wrong done by some in the community, and ahead to a cleansing (13:1). For the first hearers, it tied repentance and the leaders' houses (kingly, prophetic, priestly) to the hope of the city's survival.
views: A real past or future piercing
A person from David's house, a priest or a prophet, was killed, and the nation will mourn.
A figure for Israel's guilt
'Pierced' is a word for the wound the people inflicted on God and one another.
Christ on the cross
John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 apply it to Jesus.

traditions.q: Who is 'the one they pierced' (12:10), and who are the mourners?
views: Catholic
The Church reads the verse as John 19:37 does, of Christ crucified, and Jerome in his commentary on the Twelve reads the verse of Christ.
jerome-twelve
Orthodox

Cyril of Alexandria worked from the Septuagint, which has 'because they abused' (Hill's rendering) in this verse. He notes that the Hebrew has 'pierced,' says the sense is the same, since the Jews abused Christ and Pilate's soldiers pierced his side, and applies the verse to Christ.
cyril-twelve
swete-lxx
Reformed

Calvin takes 'pierced' as the Jews' long provocation of God, says it was made visible in Christ's pierced side (John 19:37), and reads the 'spirit of grace' as the Spirit's gift of repentance and the light of faith.
calvin-twelve
Dispensationalist

Gaebelein says the pierced One is the Lord Jesus Christ (John 19:37). He says the mourners, the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, will mourn in a future day, not in the gospel age, when Christ appears in the clouds (Matthew 24:30; Revelation 1:7).
gaebelein-zech-12-14

title: Strike the Shepherd
sum: On that day a spring will be opened for David's house and Jerusalem, for sin and impurity. The LORD will cut off the names of the idols and remove the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness (13:1-2). A man who still prophesies will be told by his own father and mother that he cannot live, and they will pierce him through. The prophets will be ashamed, drop their hairy cloaks, and deny that they are prophets; one with wounds between his hands says he got them in the house of his friends (13:3-6).

Then the poem turns: 'Sword, wake up against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me.' The shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter, and the LORD turns his hand on the little ones (13:7). Two parts of the land are cut off and die, and the third is brought through fire, refined like silver and gold, until they call on the LORD's name and he says, 'This is my people' (13:8-9). Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27 quote 13:7.
readings: Read as the end of false prophecy
13:1-6 describes a land so cleansed that its own parents punish a false prophet, and its prophets disown their craft. The law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18 is carried out to the end.
Read as the death of the shepherd and the refining of a remnant
13:7-9 is a poem on its own: the LORD himself calls the sword on the shepherd, the people are scattered and cut down to a third, and the third is purified to be his people again.
Read as a prophecy of the passion
Jesus applied 13:7 to the scattering of the disciples (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27), and the church saw in the struck shepherd the crucified Christ, and in the third the church tried by trials.

views.H: The Persian period knew conflicts between prophets and the community's leaders: Nehemiah 6:7, 14 tells of prophets hired against him, among them the prophetess Noadiah. A scatter-and-refine poem fits any of the disasters Judah suffered, but no event in this period matches.
views.C: Many scholars think 13:7-9 once stood after 11:17 ('A sword will strike his arm'), because the sword and the shepherd match and 13:1-6 interrupts; the order in the book is a later arrangement. 13:2-6 is read as a late and sharp view of prophecy. The sudden mention of 'my shepherd,' the man next to the LORD, is a puzzle, since in chapter 11 the shepherds were bad.
views.J: On 13:2-6, the end of prophecy, the Babylonian Talmud teaches that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died the Divine Spirit of prophetic revelation left Israel and only a heavenly voice remained (Yoma 9b).
views.X: Jesus quoted 13:7 on the night he was taken (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27; John 16:32 echoes it). The fathers read the shepherd as Christ, the sheep as the apostles, and the refined third as the church in trial. 13:1 is read with John 19:34 as the water and blood from his side.
views.F: Dispensationalist and other premillennial readers see 13:8-9 as Israel in the Great Tribulation, with a third saved. Others read the refining as the church's trials throughout history.

echoes: Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27; John 16:32; John 19:34; Mark 1:23; Amos 7:14; 1 Kings 18:28; 2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4; Deuteronomy 13:1-11; Deuteronomy 18:20; Ezekiel 5:1-12; Ezekiel 36:25; Isaiah 48:10; Hosea 2:23; Zechariah 12:10; Zechariah 11:17; Jeremiah 6:27-30

settings.what: The spring for sin, and the end of idols and prophets
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: David's house and the people living in Jerusalem (13:1), and the prophets and their families (13:2-6)
settings.why: To promise that the repentance of 12:10 will be met with cleansing, and that the three sources of the people's sin, idols, false prophets and an unclean spirit, will be removed. The picture of parents stabbing their own child for false prophecy is the extreme case of the law, meant to say that no one in the new land will protect falsehood. For readers in a community where prophets had been used for hire against its leaders, it told them what to expect from the day of the LORD.
views: The end of false prophecy only
The law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18 applied to the end.
The end of prophecy
A late view that the age of prophets had passed (Yoma 9b: the Holy Spirit left Israel when Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died).

settings.what: The struck shepherd and the refined third
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, speaking in the first person to the sword and of 'my shepherd'
settings.to: The sword (in the poem's address), and the community of Yehud, who hear what will happen to the shepherd, the sheep and the land
settings.why: To say that the shepherd's death and the scattering of the sheep are the LORD's doing, and that out of it a third will remain who are tested and made his people. For the hearers it explains disaster as refining, not abandonment, and ends in the covenant formula, the LORD's 'my people' and the people's 'my God.'
views: A good shepherd struck
The man next to the LORD is a good leader struck down (Christian readings: Christ).
A bad shepherd struck
The sword of 11:17 falls on the bad shepherd, and the poem has been moved.
The people's leaders in general
'Shepherd' for rulers of the nation in the time of crisis.

title: The Day the LORD Is King
sum: The book ends with one long day of the LORD. The nations gather against Jerusalem; the city is captured, the houses plundered, the women raped, and half the people go into exile (14:1-2). Then the LORD goes out to fight. His feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits from east to west, and the people flee through the new valley as they fled from the earthquake in Uzziah's day. The LORD comes with all the holy ones (14:3-5).

The day is a day without ordinary light and darkness, with light at evening. Living water flows from Jerusalem to the eastern and western seas. The LORD becomes king over all the earth, one LORD with one name; the land is leveled to a plain, and Jerusalem stands high and safe (14:6-11). A plague falls on the attackers (14:12-15). The survivors of the nations go up year by year to bow down to the King and to keep the Feast of Booths, and those who will not get no rain (14:16-19). Even the horses' bells and the cooking pots are 'Holy to the LORD,' and no Canaanite is left in the house of the LORD (14:20-21).
readings: Read as the last battle and the new age

The chapter pictures the end: the nations' final assault, the LORD's appearing, the transformation of the land, the world's worship. It joins Ezekiel 38-48, Joel 3 and the New Testament's second coming.
Read as the language of the sieges of Jerusalem

Critical readers see a poem built from the memory of 586 BC (plunder, exile, half the city taken) and a hope that the next time the LORD will intervene, written in a language that later readers used for the end.
Read as the reign of Christ and the church

Calvin and many Reformed and amillennial readers see the chapter as the reign of Christ from his ascension, with the nations coming to worship him, and the Feast of Booths and the holy pots as the language of Old Testament worship for the worship of the gospel age.

views.H: The chapter has two layers of memory: the capture of Jerusalem, with half the city taken into exile (586 BC, or later sieges), and the earthquake of Uzziah's time (about 760 BC, Amos 1:1). No known battle fits its end. The place names of 14:10 (Geba, Rimmon, the Benjamin Gate, the Tower of Hananel, the king's winepresses) are real places of Judah and Jerusalem and agree with Nehemiah 3.
views.C: Critical scholars see chapter 14 as the last addition to the book, an apocalyptic poem built from earlier sources. The text has many hard places: 14:5 (flee or be blocked), 14:6 (cold and frost), 14:18 (the extra 'not'), 14:21 (Canaanite). Hanson and others see chapters 9-14 as an early stage of apocalyptic. The view that Judah fights 'against' Jerusalem (14:14) depends on a reading of one preposition.
views.J: Zechariah 14 is the haftarah for the first day of Booths. Verse 9 is quoted in the Aleinu prayer. The Talmud tells that seventy bulls were offered at Booths for the seventy nations (Sukkah 55b), and the Mishnah records the water ceremony of the festival (Sukkah 4:9-10; 5:1).
views.X: Christians have read the Mount of Olives as the scene of the ascension (Acts 1:11-12) and the return, the living water as the Spirit (John 7:37-39) and the river of life (Revelation 22:1), and the holiness of ordinary things (14:20-21) as the sanctifying of all of life. Calvin reads the nations' worship in 14:16 of the conversion of the nations; see the cards.
views.F: Dispensationalist and other premillennial readers take 14:1-11 as the last battle and Christ's return, and 14:16-21 as the worship of the millennial kingdom. Amillennial and postmillennial readers take the chapter as fulfilled or being fulfilled in the church. The Catholic Church has rejected 'even modified forms' of an earthly messianic kingdom (Catechism 676).

deep.title: Those who came against Jerusalem go up to it (Claude's theory)
deep.b: Two Hebrew verbs of motion join the chapters. The same Hebrew phrase, habba'im 'al Yerushalaim, 'those who come against Jerusalem,' is used of the attacking nations in 12:9 and of the survivors in 14:16, who 'go up' (ya'alu) to Jerusalem year after year to worship. The movement toward the city is the same; what changes is the heart. The attackers become the pilgrims, and 'all the nations' is the enemy in 12:3 and 14:2 and the worshiper in 14:16. This puts in one phrase the common observation that the book moves from judgment of the nations to their worship (9:7, 10). It is my reading of the Hebrew wording, and I offer it as such.

echoes: Acts 1:11-12; Matthew 24:3; Luke 19:37; Ezekiel 11:23; Ezekiel 43:2; Ezekiel 47:1-12; Joel 3:18; Amos 1:1; John 7:2, 37-38; Revelation 22:1-5; Revelation 21:23-25; Revelation 22:3; Deuteronomy 6:4; Deuteronomy 16:13; Leviticus 23:34; Nehemiah 8:14-17; Exodus 28:36; John 2:14-16; Mark 11:17; Isaiah 60:19-20; Isaiah 19:19-25; Obadiah 21

settings.what: The day of the LORD: siege, appearing and the king of all the earth
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: Jerusalem ('your plunder,' said to the city) and the people of Yehud and the scattered Judeans
settings.why: To tell a small community in a city with a small wall that the worst possible siege will not be the end: the LORD himself will fight, the mountain will split to open a way, and in the end the whole earth will see him as king. The shocking details of 14:2 do not soften the loss; they make the later rescue more than a return to the old order. Knowing that the readers had lived through repeated disaster changes the weight of 'the rest of the people will not be cut off.'
views: A future final battle
Premillennial and dispensational readers: the battle and the LORD's return are still to come.
The language of the earlier sieges
A picture built from the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, told as a pattern for every siege.
The reign of Christ
Calvin and many Reformed readers: the chapter pictures Christ's kingdom.

settings.what: The plague, the Feast of Booths and the holy pots
settings.by: The LORD, through the prophet whom the book names as Zechariah (whether chapters 9-14 come from the prophet of chapters 1-8 is debated; see the book page)
settings.to: The people of Yehud and, in the story, the survivors of the nations
settings.why: To say what follows the victory: the survivors of the nations are joined to the LORD's worship at Jerusalem, and the holiness of the high priest's plate reaches everything in the city. For a small community that was proud of its Temple and fearful of foreigners in it, the last line (no Canaanite, trader or outsider in the house) is a reminder of purity. At the same time, the nations are worshipers, not only victims.
views: Literal worship in a millennial temple
The feast and the sacrifices will be kept in the age to come.
The language of worship for the gospel age
Temple and feast are the Old Testament's way of saying that all nations will worship the LORD.
A promise of a purified Temple
The last verse means no trading or alien uses in the house (compare John 2:14-16).

traditions.q: Is the LORD's return to the Mount of Olives (14:4) still to come, and will the nations' war and the millennial kingdom follow?
views: Catholic
The Church has rejected 'even modified forms' of the hope that the messianic kingdom will be realized within history, under the name of millenarianism (Catechism 676).
catechism-catholic
Lutheran

The Augsburg Confession (Article 17) says that Christ will return to judge and condemns those who teach that the godly will take possession of the kingdom of the world before the resurrection of the dead.
augsburg
Reformed

Calvin takes the standing of the LORD's feet on the Mount of Olives (14:4) as figurative language for God's power in rescuing his afflicted Church, as if he watched the battle from the mountain; he calls the allegorical readings (Christ's ascension from the mountain, the apostles going out through the split mountain) refinements with nothing solid in them.
calvin-twelve
Baptist
The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) teaches that Jesus Christ will return personally and visibly in glory to the earth, without fixing a view of the millennium.
baptist-faith-message-2000-last-things
Dispensationalist

Gaebelein says the LORD's feet will stand "in that day" on the Mount of Olives, and the mountain will split in the middle to make a valley for escape. He calls the Feast of Booths in 14:16-19 "the millennial feast."
gaebelein-zech-12-14

traditions.q: Will the Feast of Booths and its sacrifices be kept in the age to come (14:16-21)?
views: Dispensationalist

Gaebelein says the temple will stand in Jerusalem during the Millennium as a house of prayer for all nations, and that sacrifices will be brought in it. He also says there will still be disobedience among the nations in the kingdom age.
gaebelein-zech-12-14
Reformed

The feast, the pots and the sacrifices are the Old Testament way of describing the worship of all nations under Christ, since the sacrifices ended in his once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10); Calvin takes the nations' coming up to worship at the feast (14:16) of the conversion of the nations to the God of Israel, seen in the many churches formed in the world.
calvin-twelve
